1.q: וַ⁠תְּדַבֵּ֨ר מִרְיָ֤ם וְ⁠אַהֲרֹן֙ בְּ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה עַל־אֹד֛וֹת הָ⁠אִשָּׁ֥ה הַ⁠כֻּשִׁ֖ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לָקָ֑ח כִּֽי־אִשָּׁ֥ה כֻשִׁ֖ית לָקָֽח
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Now Moses had taken a woman, a Cushitess. And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses on account of this woman, this Cushitess]

Some scholars argue that this woman was Zipporah, whom Moses married in Exodus 2:21. Other scholars argue that this is another woman to whom Moses was also married. It is recommended that you do not identify this woman beyond identifying her as a **Cushitess**.

Here, the word **Cushitess** refers to a woman from the area south of Egypt, sometimes known as Nubia. This is modern day southern Egypt and northern Sudan. Alternate translation: [the one from Cush … one from Cush]

2.q: הֲ⁠רַ֤ק אַךְ־בְּ⁠מֹשֶׁה֙ דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הֲ⁠לֹ֖א גַּם־בָּ֣⁠נוּ דִבֵּ֑ר
2.note: Aaron and Miriam are using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Yahweh did not only speak in Moses. He also spoke in us!]

The phrases **in Moses** and **in us** are common expressions of this culture that mean “by means of Moses” and “by means of us.” If these phrases do not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by means of Moses … by means of us]
By **in us**, Miriam and Aaron mean themselves but not Moses to whom they are referring, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

3.q: וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ מֹשֶׁ֖ה ענו מְאֹ֑ד מִ⁠כֹּל֙ הָֽ⁠אָדָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אֲדָמָֽה
3.note: Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. The ULT indicates this with parentheses. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now it is important to know that the man Moses was very meek, more than the man who was upon the face of the ground]

The author is not referring to a specific **man**. The author means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any human]

The author is using **upon the face of the ground** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in the world” or “on the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who was alive] or [who was in the world]

Here, **the face of the ground** represents the surface of the ground. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the land] or [the land]

4.note: In a context such as this, your language might say “approach” instead of **go**. The tent was in the middle of the camp, not outside it. See how you translated the similar expression in 11:26. Alternate translation: [Approach … And the three of them approached]

By **the three of them went out**, the author means they went out to the tent of meeting. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the three of them went out to the tent of meeting]

5.note: Here, the author is speaking as if **Yahweh** had actually moved physically downward. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:25. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh met them]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **cloud** that is in the shape of **a pillar**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a cloud in the shape of a pillar]

The author is speaking of the cloud column as if it were a living thing that could **stand**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had it stay]

In a context such as this, your language might say “approached” instead of **went out**. The tent was in the middle of the camp, not outside it. See how you translated the similar expression in 12:4. Alternate translation: [and the two of them approached]

6.note: Here, **words** represents what God will say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I am about to say]

6.q: אִם־יִֽהְיֶה֙ נְבִ֣יאֲ⁠כֶ֔ם יְהוָ֗ה בַּ⁠מַּרְאָה֙ אֵלָ֣י⁠ו אֶתְוַדָּ֔ע
6.note: Yahweh is describing a possible condition in which he will make himself known in a vision only if there is a prophet of Yahweh. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that there is a prophet of yours of Yahweh. In that case, in the vision I will make myself known to him]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **prophet** who belongs to and speaks for **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a prophet among you through whom I speak]
Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [of mine]

These two phrases **in the vision I will make myself known to him** and **In the dream I will speak with him** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [in the vision or the dream I will reveal myself to him]

Here, **vision** and **dream** represent supernatural revelations in general, not specific visions or dreams. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in a vision … In a dream]

Here the masculine terms **to him** and **with him** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [to that person … with that person]

7.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Not so do I make myself known to my servant Moses]

Here, the phrase **he himself is faithful** could indicate that: (1) Moses faithfully does what God requires. Alternate translation: [in all my house he, he acts faithfully] (2) Moses is entrusted with the **house**. Alternate translation: [with all my house he, he is entrusted]

God is using the term **house** to mean all the people who serve and worship him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among all my people]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he is faithful** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Moses is very faithful. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that emphasis. Alternate translation: [he certainly is faithful]

8.note: Yahweh is using **mouth to mouth** as a common expression of his culture to mean “face to face” or “directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Face to face] or [Directly]

By **appearance and not in riddles**, Yahweh means that he spoke to Moses plainly and directly rather than in ways that were difficult to understand. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and clearly instead of in complicated ways]

By **the form of Yahweh**, Yahweh means the visible way in which he reveals himself. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the visible way in which Yahweh reveals himself]
Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [my form]

8.q: וּ⁠מַדּ֨וּעַ֙ לֹ֣א יְרֵאתֶ֔ם לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר בְּ⁠עַבְדִּ֥⁠י בְ⁠מֹשֶֽׁה
8.note: God is using the question form to rebuke Aaron and Miriam. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So you should fear to speak against my servant, against Moses.]

It might seem that the expression **against my servant, against Moses** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [against my servant Moses]

9.note: The phrase **the nose of Yahweh burned** is a common expression of this culture that means that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh’s anger burned against them] or [and Yahweh was enraged with them]

The implication is that Yahweh left the sacred tent where he had been speaking with Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he left the sacred tent]

10.note: The author is speaking of the **cloud** as if it were a living thing that could move away on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had the cloud depart]

The author is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And look … and look]

The point of this comparison is that just as **snow** is white, so was her skin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [white like snow] or [white like wool]

The author is not referring to a specific **snow**. He means snow in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like snow]

It might seem that the expression **she was with a skin disease** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, since the author stated it earlier in the verse. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he saw what had happened]

11.note: Aaron uses two words that mean **please** to indicate his own low status and the urgency of his request. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [I beg you, my lord,]

Aaron is referring to Moses by the respectful title **my lord**. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 11:28. Alternate translation: [my master] or [my leader]

Here, Aaron is speaking as if sin were actually something that could be **put upon** a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not make us suffer the punishment for the sin]
By **us**, Aaron means himself and Miriam but not Moses to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The expression **which we did foolishly and which we sinned** expresses a single idea. The word **foolishly** tells more about **sinned**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [which we foolishly sinned] or [which we did so foolishly]

12.q: אַל־נָ֥א תְהִ֖י כַּ⁠מֵּ֑ת אֲשֶׁ֤ר בְּ⁠צֵאת⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠רֶ֣חֶם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֵּאָכֵ֖ל חֲצִ֥י בְשָׂרֽ⁠וֹ
12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **one having died** has decaying flesh, so Miriam has decaying flesh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [May her skin not be like the skin of the one having died, who, when he comes out from the womb of his mother, then half of his flesh was eaten]

The author is using **when he comes out from the womb of his mother** as a common expression of his culture to mean “when he is born.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he is born]

The expression **was eaten** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [then half of his flesh has wasted away] or [then half of his flesh has rotted]

13.note: Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

Here Moses repeats the word **please** to show that he is speaking humbly and pleading urgently with God. To show humility and urgency in your language, you may need to use different words or expressions rather than repeating “please.” See how you translated the similar repetition in 12:11. Alternate translation: [God, I respectfully and urgently ask you,]

14.q: וְ⁠אָבִ֨י⁠הָ֙ יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙ בְּ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ הֲ⁠לֹ֥א תִכָּלֵ֖ם שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים
14.note: The author is using the question form to emphasize that being spit in the face by her father would certainly humiliate her for seven days. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And her father, spitting, spit in her face, she would be humiliated seven days.]

14.q: וְ⁠אָבִ֨י⁠הָ֙ יָרֹ֤ק יָרַק֙ בְּ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠הָ הֲ⁠לֹ֥א תִכָּלֵ֖ם שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים
14.note: The author says **And her father, spitting, spit in her face, would she not be humiliated seven days** to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain how long Miriam should be isolated outside the camp. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [Imagine that her father, spitting, spit in her face. In that case, would she not be humiliated seven days]

Spitting **in her face** was a symbolic action by which her father showed that she was disgraced and unclean. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And her father humiliated her by spitting in her face]

The author is repeating forms of the verb **spit** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [spit directly]

The expression **would she not be humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [would that not cause humiliation for her]

The expression **she shall be shut up** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelites. Alternate translation: [You Israelites must shut her up]

The implication is that she must be excluded from the camp, not that she must be locked up. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [She shall be banished]

The phrase **from outside to the camp** is a common expression of this culture to mean “in the area outside the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the area outside the camp]

The expression **she shall be gathered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar construction in 11:30. Alternate translation: [And she shall return]

15.note: The expression **was shut up** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites shut up Miriam]

The implication is that Miriam was shut up outside the camp, not that she was locked up. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [And Miriam was banished]

The phrase **from outside to the camp** is a common expression of this culture that means “in the area away from the camp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 12:14. Alternate translation: [in the area outside the camp]

The expression **was gathered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in 12:14. Alternate translation: [until Miriam returned]

16.note: The word **Hazeroth** is the name of a place in the desert. See how you translated this name in 11:35.

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **wilderness** that is characterized by being near **Paran**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:12. Alternate translation: [in the wilderness that was near Paran]
